info.title: Fractal JDT LS endpoint
info.summary: One JDT LS shared by many LLM sessions, each in its own Git worktree, through a token-gated REST API on localhost.
info.description:
Fractal JDT LS's HTTP endpoint: one Eclipse JDT Language Server shared by many sessions, each working in its own Git worktree of a Maven project. The endpoint runs inside JDT LS. This description is its contract, and every operation's description is written to be read by an LLM.

## Calling it

- Every operation is a `POST` with a JSON body, except `GET /v1/status` and `GET /v1/openapi.json`.
- Send `Authorization: Bearer <token>` and `Host: 127.0.0.1:<port>`, and no `Origin` header. `X-Fractal-Session: <your session's id>` is optional, and recorded only in the endpoint's log.
- Every call blocks until its work is done. There's nothing to poll, except after `worktrees/add` with `wait: false`.
- Unknown request fields are refused with `invalid-request`. Ignore response fields you don't know.

## The worktree and the module

Every operation on code names, in its body:

- `worktree`: the absolute path of a registered worktree's root (see `worktrees/add`);
- `module`: the folder of the Maven module you're working in, relative to that root, such as `harness-app`, or `.` for the root POM.

The module is where a request starts. Results never come from another worktree, and an edit never touches another worktree's files. A search or rename covers the module and the modules of the same worktree that depend on it. Files in requests and results are relative to their module. Paths in `sync` and in diffs are relative to the worktree.

## Addressing code

Name a declaration with a Java name (the `JavaName` schema), and code without a name with a text anchor (the `TextAnchor` schema). Results use 1-based lines and columns, with the source line. LSP's 0-based positions appear only in the LSP passthrough.

## The disk is the truth

Edit files however you like: your own tools, `git checkout`, `sed`, generators. You don't need to tell the endpoint. Before every operation that depends on code, it reconciles JDT LS with the disk for the module's whole worktree (a "fixed point"), and reports what it found in `sync`. When nothing changed, it takes a fast path that costs milliseconds. The fixed point refreshes, builds and joins Eclipse's jobs; it never guesses from timing.

## Errors

Every error is an RFC 9457 problem (`application/problem+json`) with a stable `code`, a `detail` in your terms, and a `hint` saying what to do next.

- When there's a choice to make, `candidates` lists the choices. Each candidate's `set` maps JSON Pointers into your request to new values: apply one candidate's `set` (creating any object missing on the way), then send the request again. A candidate always fits the operation that returned it.
- `retryable: true` means the same request may succeed later. Wait `retryAfter` seconds first, when it's given.
- The `ErrorCode` schema is the catalogue: every code, its HTTP status, when it happens, and what to do. `components.examples` has an example of each, named `error-<code>`, and forms specific to some operations, such as `error-file-in-other-module-file`, whose candidates fit those operations' requests.

## Waiting and timeouts

JDT LS takes a few seconds to start, and a worktree's import takes from seconds to minutes. **Imports run alone:** while any worktree is being added, every other request waits. Until JDT LS is ready, and during an import, a request waits (`wait: true`, the default), or gets `not-ready` with `retryAfter` (`wait: false`). Every request has a timeout (`timeoutMs`, with a default per operation). The wait counts towards it. When it passes, the endpoint cancels the work and returns `timeout`. A caller that disconnects isn't noticed, so its work goes on until its timeout: send a `timeoutMs` no longer than you will wait.

The endpoint runs up to 16 operations at once and queues up to 64 more, in order. A request beyond them gets `busy` at once, with `retryAfter`.

## What the endpoint fixes

Its contract depends on these, so the harness can't change them. The endpoint refuses to start with a settings file that sets them otherwise:

- `java.autobuild.enabled: false`: each fixed point builds explicitly;
- `java.configuration.updateBuildConfiguration: disabled`: the endpoint sends changed POMs through m2e itself;
- the client capabilities `workspace.applyEdit: false` and `workspace.didChangeWatchedFiles.dynamicRegistration: false`.

JDT LS writes no `.project`, `.classpath` or `.settings/` into worktrees.

post.summary: Shut JDT LS down
post.description:
Answers first, then shuts JDT LS down through LSP `shutdown` and `exit`, so it saves its workspace state, and the process exits. Requests after this get `shutting-down`. Calling it again answers the same.

**When to use it:** when the harness is done with this process. Registered worktrees are saved, and restored on the next start with the same `-data`.

post.summary: Add a Git worktree, and import its Maven modules
post.description:
Registers a worktree and imports its Maven modules into JDT LS, each as its own Eclipse project. The call blocks until the import is done and every module passed the health check. If a module fails it, the endpoint repairs the import once (removing and adding the worktree again), and reports it in `worktree.repair`.

**Imports run alone:** while this runs, every other request waits. A large worktree can take a minute or more.

**When to use it:** before any other operation on the worktree. Adding a registered worktree again is harmless (`added: false`), and waits for its import if one is running.

**Errors:**
- `not-a-worktree`: pass the worktree's root, the folder `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` prints.
- `worktree-name-in-use`: another registered worktree has the same folder name; remove it first.
- `worktree-nested`: the worktree is inside a registered one, or contains one; worktrees must sit side by side.
- `import-failed`: the repair didn't help; remove the worktree and add it again, then report it.
- `not-ready` with `wait: false`, or when `timeoutMs` passed: the import started and carries on; add it again with `wait: true` to wait for it.

post.summary: Remove a worktree from JDT LS
post.description:
Deletes the worktree's Eclipse projects, without deleting any file, and removes them from m2e's registry. A worktree already deleted from disk can be removed.

**When to use it:** when no session works in the worktree any more, and before adding another worktree with the same folder name.

**Errors:** `worktree-not-registered`: it isn't registered; the candidates are the registered ones.

While it runs, as while a worktree is imported, other requests that reach JDT LS wait: the removal takes a second or two.

post.summary: Check that a module can be addressed
post.description:
Maps `worktree` and `module` to the module's project, with exactly the checks every operation on a module makes, and returns the module. It changes nothing, and is answered from JDT LS's workspace, so it waits while a worktree is imported, like every request that reaches JDT LS.

The checks: the worktree is registered, and its folder is still there; the module's `pom.xml` exists; JDT LS has a project for it, which passes the import health check (at the module's own folder, with m2e's facade and, unless its packaging is `pom`, the Java nature); and the agent placed that project in this worktree, which a stray `.git` between the worktree's root and the module would break.

**When to use it:** to find out whether a module is ready for other operations, or why it isn't.

**Errors:**
- `worktree-not-registered`, `module-not-found`: use a candidate, or add the worktree first.
- `module-not-imported`: its `pom.xml` came after the import; see the hint.
- `module-in-other-worktree`: remove the stray `.git` that `detail` names, then remove the worktree and add it again.
- `import-failed`: remove the worktree and add it again.
- `not-ready`: wait `retryAfter` seconds and retry, or send `wait: true`.

post.description:

**When to use it:** after editing files, to see what's broken. You never need to say which files you changed.

**Errors:**

- `not-ready`: wait `retryAfter` seconds and retry, or send `wait: true`.

post.summary: Where an element is declared
post.description:
Returns the declaration of the element at a text anchor, or of a named element. Library and JDK elements come back with `library` instead of a file.

A name may be of a library or JDK element too, such as `java.lang.Math#max(int,int)`: a name that matches nothing in the worktree's sources is looked up on the module's classpath (see `JavaName`).

**When to use it:** to find what a name in the code refers to.

**Errors:**
- `ambiguous-member`, `ambiguous-type`: apply the candidate you mean.
- `type-not-found`, `member-not-found`: check the name, or use a candidate.
- `text-not-found`, `text-not-unique`: copy the text exactly from the file, add `within` from a candidate, or make `text` longer.
- `not-applicable`: the element is the wrong kind; `detail` says what's needed.
- `worktree-not-registered`, `module-not-found`: use a candidate, or add the worktree first.
- `not-ready`: wait `retryAfter` seconds and retry, or send `wait: true`.

post.summary: Inline a local variable
post.description:
Replaces every use of a local variable with its initializer, and removes the declaration.

The endpoint computes the edit with JDT from the files as its fixed point left them: that's the edit's baseline. Then it applies it as one more fixed point, under Eclipse's workspace lock: it checks that no file the edit reads or creates changed since the baseline, writes every file of the edit or none, builds, and returns a unified diff and the worktree's problems. No other request sees the files half written. Files keep their charset, byte order, byte order mark and line separators, and nothing outside the edit's text changes. `dryRun: true` returns the diff without writing. Git is the undo.

**The operation folder.** Once the request's first fixed point is done (so the folder's own files don't make it a full one), the endpoint records the refactoring in `<worktree>/temp/fractal-jdtls/<operation>/`, with an ID it generates: `request.json` (the ID, the time received, the operation and this request's body), `diff.patch` (the full diff, once the edit is computed, before any file is written), and last `response.json`, this answer as sent, success or problem (written to a temporary name and renamed). A successful answer gives `operation` and `operationFolder`. If an answer is lost, find the folder by `request.json`: with `response.json` that's the outcome. Without it, the outcome is unknown: while `GET /v1/status` lists the `operation` in `inFlight`, it's still running; otherwise it stopped without answering, and the files `diff.patch` names, with Git, show what was written. The endpoint never reads the folders back or removes them: ignore `temp/` in Git, and clean them up when you choose. A `temp` or `temp/fractal-jdtls` that's a symbolic link, out of the worktree or inside it, is `edit-outside-worktree`, nothing written.

**Checking an apply against its dry run:** send the dry run's `writeSetDigest` as `expectWriteSetDigest`.

**Errors:**
- `ambiguous-member`, `ambiguous-type`: apply the candidate you mean.
- `type-not-found`, `member-not-found`: check the name, or use a candidate.
- `text-not-found`, `text-not-unique`: copy the text exactly from the file, add `within` from a candidate, or make `text` longer.
- `not-applicable`: the element is the wrong kind; `detail` says what's needed.
- `files-changed`: another session changed a file meanwhile; send the same request again.
- `edit-changed`: the edit computed now isn't the one `expectWriteSetDigest` names; nothing was written. Review its `diff`, and send `writeSetDigest` to apply it.
- `write-failed`: a file couldn't be written, and every file was put back; fix what `detail` names (such as a file's permissions), then send the same request again.
- `refactoring-refused`: JDT's reason is in `detail`; change the request accordingly.
- `worktree-not-registered`, `module-not-found`: use a candidate, or add the worktree first.
- `not-ready`: wait `retryAfter` seconds and retry, or send `wait: true`.

bearer.description: The token the harness gave the launcher in `FRACTAL_JDTLS_HTTP_TOKEN`, at least 32 characters.

Session.name: X-Fractal-Session
Session.description: Optional: your session's identifier. Recorded only in the endpoint's log.

RetryAfter.description: Seconds to wait, as in the problem's `retryAfter`.

WorktreePath.description: The absolute path of a worktree's root: the folder that holds its `.git` (a folder for a main checkout, a file for a linked worktree). The endpoint resolves symbolic links, and reports the resolved path.

ModulePath.description: The folder holding a Maven module's `pom.xml`, relative to the worktree's root, with `/` separators: `harness-app`, `services/billing`, or `.` for the root POM. No leading `/`, no `..`.

JavaName.description:
A Java name for a declaration: in the worktree's sources, or, for a read-only operation, on the requesting module's classpath.

- A type: `com.acme.Foo`. A nested type: `com.acme.Foo.Bar` (`com.acme.Foo$Bar` works too).
- A method: `com.acme.Foo#bar`, or with its parameter types, `com.acme.Foo#bar(int,java.lang.String)`.
- A constructor: the type's simple name as the member, `com.acme.Foo#Foo(int)`.
- A field or an enum constant: `com.acme.Foo#count`.
- A package: `com.acme`.

Rules:

- **Parameter types are optional.** Without them, a name that matches several overloads is `ambiguous-member`, which lists every overload: pass one back. `bar()` means no parameters.
- **Parameter types** are comma-separated, and whitespace is ignored. Each may be simple (`String`) or fully qualified (`java.lang.String`). Type arguments are ignored (`List<String>` is `List`). Arrays are `int[]`, and varargs `String...`, which is the same as `String[]`.
- **A field wins a name without parentheses:** `com.acme.Foo#size` is the field `size` if `Foo` declares one; a method that shares a field's name is written with its parentheses, `com.acme.Foo#size()`.
- **Ambiguous:** a simple parameter type that matches two types (`Date` for `java.util.Date` and `java.sql.Date`). A fully qualified parameter type matches only that type.
- **Library and JDK elements** (`java.lang.Math#max(int,int)`) can be named in the read-only operations (definition, references, implementations, type-hierarchy, call-hierarchy, describe). A name that matches nothing in the worktree's sources is looked up on the requesting module's classpath: its Maven dependencies and the JDK. Refactorings only ever address the worktree's own sources.
- **No name here:** anonymous classes, lambdas and local variables. Address them with a `TextAnchor`.
- **The fully qualified form** that results and errors use always resolves.

TextAnchor.title: TextAnchor
TextAnchor.description:
Code addressed by its text, like an editor's `old_string`. Use it for code without a Java name: a local variable, an expression, statements to extract, or a use of a library element.

For example, `{"file": "src/main/java/org/fractal/harness/app/Greeter.java", "text": "int width = 10 - clean.length();", "select": "width"}` is the local variable `width`, at its declaration.

Text found nowhere is `text-not-found`. Text found more than once is `text-not-unique`, which lists every occurrence and, where `within` tells them apart, candidates.

file.description: The Java source file, relative to the request's module, with `/` separators.

text.description: The exact source text, character for character, including whitespace and indentation. A line break matches `\n` or `\r\n`. It must occur exactly once in the file, or exactly once within `within`. Copy it from the file as it is now.

within.description: Optional. The Java name of a type or member declared in `file`. `text` is then looked for only inside that declaration's source. Use it when `text-not-unique` offers it as a candidate.

select.description: Optional. The part of `text` that the operation acts on, which must occur exactly once inside `text`. By default, all of `text`. Operations that act on one element (definition, references, rename, describe, hierarchies, inline) use the element at `select`. Extract operations use exactly the selected source.

CodeTarget.title: CodeTarget
CodeTarget.description: What the operation acts on: a Java name (a string), or a text anchor (an object).

ElementKind.description: The kind of a Java element.

Location.title: Location
Location.description: Where a declaration or a use is, in the caller's terms. Code in the worktree has `module`, `file`, a range and the source line; a library element has `library` instead.

element.description: The Java name of the declaration here (for a definition), or of the declaration that encloses this code (for a reference or a call). A library element's name can be passed back as the target of a read-only operation.

file.description: The file, relative to `module`. Absent for a library element.

endColumn.description: 1-based column just after the range's end.

source.description: The source line at `line`, without its line break; long lines end with … after 500 characters.

library.description: For an element of a library or the JDK: the jar's path, or `jrt:/<module>` for the JDK.

Sync.title: Sync
Sync.description: What the fixed point before this answer found and cost. Before every operation that depends on code, the endpoint reconciles JDT LS with the disk for the request's whole worktree: the fast path's check, then (unless it skips) a refresh, m2e's update of changed POMs, an incremental build, and a join of the jobs that scheduled. You never need to tell the endpoint what you changed: this report shows what it found. A request whose worktree has another request's fixed point running waits for it, and then decides: the fast path is never taken while one runs, and no answer is read while one changes the markers.

skipped.description: `true` when the fast path found nothing changed in the worktree, so the endpoint skipped the refresh, the build and the join. The answer is still up to date.

notSkippedBecause.description: Why the full fixed point ran, when `skipped` is `false`: `disk-changed` (files changed, added or deleted on disk), `status-changed` (a change that kept its modification time), `eclipse-changed` (a change made inside JDT LS since the last fixed point), `changed-paths` (the request named `changedPaths`), `first` (the worktree's first fixed point since it was added or JDT LS started), `build` (`build` never takes the fast path), `edit-applied` (the fixed point after writing a refactoring's edit).

cleanBuild.description: Present when the fixed point cleaned the worktree's projects before building them all: `requested` (`build` with `clean: true`), or `no-saved-record` (the worktree's first fixed point after a restart found no saved record of its files to compare with, so it couldn't trust what Eclipse had built; slower, once).

filesChanged.description: The files the fixed point found changed, and made JDT LS take in: at most 200, sorted by path. Changes that kept the file's modification time (`cp -p`, `touch -r`) are found too, from the file's status-change time, size and inode, and taken in without touching the file. Left out: build output, `.git`, and JDT LS's own project files (`.project`, `.classpath`, `.settings/`), which it keeps under its `-data`, not in the worktree.

filesChangedCount.description: How many files changed in all.

pomsUpdated.description: The modules whose `pom.xml` changed, and went through m2e's project update.

checkMs.description: Milliseconds for the fast path's check. 0 when it didn't run.

ruleWaitMs.description: Milliseconds spent waiting for Eclipse's workspace rule, which another worktree's import, build or fixed point may hold. Large values mean another worktree was busy.

refreshMs.description: Milliseconds refreshing the worktree from disk.

joinMs.description: Milliseconds joining the jobs the fixed point scheduled.

totalMs.description: Milliseconds for the whole fixed point.

Problem.title: Problem
Problem.description: A problem from Eclipse's markers, read after the build. Positions are 1-based; `column` counts characters.

kind.description: `java`: the compiler. `build-path`: the module's classpath, such as a missing dependency. `maven`: the POM. `other`: any other Eclipse problem.

file.description: Relative to `module`. Absent for a problem on the module as a whole.

element.description: The declaration enclosing the problem, when there is one.

ProblemCounts.title: ProblemCounts
ProblemCounts.description: How many problems of each severity the scope has, before `severities` and `limit`.

set.description: JSON Pointers into your request, each with the value to put there. Apply them all (creating any object missing on the way), then send the request again.

about.description: What this choice is, to help you choose. Not for passing back. For an element of a library or the JDK, it says `from the classpath`.

within.description: The declaration that encloses this occurrence.

ErrorCode.title: ErrorCode
ErrorCode.description: The error catalogue. Each code's HTTP status is in `x-status`, and whether retrying the same request may help in `x-retryable`. `x-candidates: true` marks codes whose problems carry `candidates`.

oneOf.title: The request is malformed
oneOf.description:
The body isn't JSON, isn't an object, misses a required field, has a field of the wrong type or value, or has a field the operation doesn't define. `errors` lists each one, by JSON Pointer.

What to do: Fix the fields `errors` names, then send the request again.

oneOf.title: The Java name isn't valid
oneOf.description:
A Java name doesn't follow the `JavaName` syntax. `detail` says where it breaks.

What to do: Write the name as the `JavaName` schema describes, for example `com.acme.Foo#bar(int)`.

oneOf.title: The request body is too large
oneOf.description:
The body is over the endpoint's limit of 1 MiB.

What to do: Send less: a shorter `text`, or fewer `changedPaths`.

oneOf.title: Unauthorized
oneOf.description:
The `Authorization: Bearer` token is missing or wrong. The problem says no more than that.

What to do: Use the token the endpoint was started with. It isn't something an LLM can fix: report it.

oneOf.title: The Host header isn't allowed
oneOf.description:
`Host` isn't `127.0.0.1:<port>`, for example `localhost:<port>`.

What to do: Connect to `127.0.0.1` with the port from the port file, and send that as `Host`.

oneOf.title: Requests with an Origin header are refused
oneOf.description:
The request has an `Origin` header, as a browser page's would. Refused, so that no web page can reach the endpoint.

What to do: Call the endpoint from a program, not a browser, and send no `Origin` header.

oneOf.title: No such operation
oneOf.description:
The path isn't one of the description's operations.

What to do: Use a path from this description: `GET /v1/openapi.json` lists them all.

oneOf.title: Wrong HTTP method
oneOf.description:
The path exists, but not with this method: operations are `POST`, and only `/v1/status` and `/v1/openapi.json` are `GET`.

What to do: Send the request with the method this description gives for the path.

oneOf.title: The worktree isn't registered
oneOf.description:
`worktree` isn't the root of a worktree added with `worktrees/add`. The candidates are the registered worktrees.

What to do: Add it with `POST /v1/worktrees/add`, or use one of the candidates.

oneOf.title: The worktree's folder is gone
oneOf.description:
The worktree is registered, but its folder no longer exists on disk.

What to do: Remove it with `POST /v1/worktrees/remove`. If it was moved, add it again at its new path.

oneOf.title: No Maven module there
oneOf.description:
There's no `pom.xml` in `module`'s folder. The candidates are the worktree's modules.

What to do: Use one of the candidates, or `.` for the root POM.

oneOf.title: The module isn't imported
oneOf.description:
The folder has a `pom.xml`, but JDT LS has no project for it: usually a module added to the build after the worktree was added, and not yet taken in.

What to do: Run `POST /v1/build` on the worktree's root module (`.`), so the endpoint takes in the changed POMs. If it's still missing, remove the worktree and add it again.

oneOf.title: The module's project belongs to another worktree
oneOf.description:
The project JDT LS has for this folder was placed in a different worktree, usually because a stray `.git` (such as `/tmp/.git`) sits nearer the module than the worktree's own. `detail` names both.

What to do: Remove the stray `.git` named in `detail`, then remove the worktree and add it again. Don't work around it: results would come from the wrong worktree.

oneOf.title: The worktree's import failed
oneOf.description:
A module failed the import health check (its project isn't at its own folder, or lacks m2e's facade or the Java nature), and the endpoint's one repair didn't fix it. `modules` lists each failing module and why. Requests on the worktree's modules get this too.

What to do: Remove the worktree and add it again. If it fails again, report it with the `modules` list: it's a JDT LS problem the endpoint couldn't repair.

oneOf.title: Not a Git worktree root
oneOf.description:
`worktree` doesn't exist, isn't absolute, or isn't the root of a Git worktree (a folder that directly holds `.git`, either a folder or a linked worktree's file).

What to do: Pass the absolute path of the worktree's root, the folder `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` prints.

oneOf.title: Another worktree has that folder name
oneOf.description:
A registered worktree has the same folder name. Folder names must be unique among the worktrees that share one JDT LS, because Eclipse's project names start with them. `detail` names the other.

What to do: Remove the other worktree first, or use a worktree whose folder has another name. This is the harness's rule to keep.

oneOf.title: The worktree overlaps a registered one
oneOf.description:
The worktree is inside a registered worktree, or contains one. Worktrees that share a JDT LS can't be nested: JDT LS imports every POM under a worktree's root, and removing a worktree deletes every project under it. `detail` names the registered worktree.

What to do: Use worktrees that sit side by side, not one inside another, such as workmux's `<repo>__worktrees/` folders. If you mean to replace the registered one, remove it first.

oneOf.title: No such file
oneOf.description:
The file doesn't exist in the module's folder.

What to do: Check the path. It's relative to the module, such as `src/main/java/com/acme/Foo.java`.

oneOf.title: The file belongs to another module
oneOf.description:
The file is inside a different module than the request's (for example, a file of `harness-app` named from the root module `.`). The candidate names the right module and the file relative to it.

What to do: Apply the candidate: it sets `module` and the file's path together.

oneOf.title: Not a Java source file
oneOf.description:
The file isn't a `.java` file on one of the module's source folders: for example, a resource, a file in `target/`, or a source folder Maven doesn't know.

What to do: Name a Java file under one of the module's source folders, such as `src/main/java`.

oneOf.title: No such type in this worktree
oneOf.description:
No type with that name is declared in the worktree's sources, nor, for a read-only operation, on the requesting module's classpath. Refactorings only address the worktree's sources, so a library type is `type-not-found` there. The candidates are types in the worktree with the same simple name, if any.

What to do: Check the package, or use a candidate. A library type can be named only in read-only operations; to change code that uses it, address that code.

oneOf.title: No such member
oneOf.description:
The type exists, but has no member with that name and those parameter types. The candidates are the type's members with that name (every overload), or, if there are none, with that name in another case.

What to do: Use one of the candidates. Members inherited from a supertype are named on the supertype.

oneOf.title: No such package
oneOf.description:
No package with that name has sources in the worktree.

What to do: Check the name. A package is named without a `#`, such as `com.acme`.

oneOf.title: The name matches several members
oneOf.description:
The name matches several overloads (a name without parentheses, when the type has no field of that name), or a simple parameter type matches several types. The candidates are every match, in the fully qualified form.

What to do: Choose the candidate you mean and send the request again with it.

oneOf.title: Two modules declare that type
oneOf.description:
Two modules of the worktree declare a type with the same fully qualified name, and the request's module neither declares it nor has exactly one of them on its classpath (a `pom` module, such as `.`, has no classpath). The candidates set `module` to each declaring module.

What to do: Choose the module whose type you mean.

oneOf.title: An import has several choices
oneOf.description:
Organize imports found a simple name that several types could be imported for. The candidates set `choices` for each, one candidate per type.

What to do: Apply one candidate for each simple name listed, then send the request again.

oneOf.title: The text isn't in the file
oneOf.description:
`text` doesn't occur in the file (or within `within`). If it occurs with different whitespace, the candidates set `text` to the file's exact text; otherwise there are none, and `detail` quotes the file's lines closest to the text's first line.

What to do: Read the file again and copy the text exactly, or apply a candidate.

oneOf.title: The text occurs more than once
oneOf.description:
`text` occurs more than once in the file (or within `within`). `occurrences` lists each, with its line and enclosing member. Where the enclosing members differ, the candidates add `within`.

What to do: Apply a candidate, or make `text` longer, with enough of the surrounding code to occur once.

oneOf.title: The operation doesn't apply to that element
oneOf.description:
The element is the wrong kind for the operation: for example, `implementations` of a field, `call-hierarchy` of a type, `extract-constant` of an expression that isn't constant, or `inline-variable` of a field. `detail` says what the operation needs.

What to do: Address an element of the kind `detail` names.

oneOf.title: Rename from the declaring module
oneOf.description:
A rename was asked from a module that doesn't declare the element. A rename covers the requesting module and the modules that depend on it, so it must start where the element is declared. The candidate sets `module` to that module.

What to do: Apply the candidate and send the request again.

oneOf.title: JDT refused the refactoring
oneOf.description:
JDT's own checks refused it: for example, a rename that would clash with an existing name, or statements that can't be extracted as a method. `detail` quotes JDT's reason. The endpoint refuses an edit in the same way when it can't apply it exactly: a file that isn't valid in its charset, or a file the edit means to make as its own (such as a package rename's `.temp`) that already exists. Nothing was written.

What to do: Change the request as JDT's reason says, such as another name.

oneOf.title: The edit would change files outside the worktree
oneOf.description:
The edit JDT computed would change a file outside the request's worktree, or a library. Files are compared by where they really are, so a file or folder of the worktree that is a symbolic link to somewhere outside it is outside too. The endpoint never changes such a file, so it refused the whole edit, and nothing was written. A refactoring's operation folder must be exactly `<the worktree's real root>/temp/fractal-jdtls/<operation>`: a `temp` that's a symbolic link, to anywhere, is refused. `files` lists them.

What to do: If a symbolic link in the worktree leads out of it, edit through the file it links to, in its own worktree; otherwise report it: this shouldn't happen when every module of the worktree is imported.

oneOf.title: The edit isn't the one expected
oneOf.description:
An apply sent `expectWriteSetDigest`, and the edit the endpoint computed from the files as they are now has another `writeSetDigest`: a file of the edit changed since the dry run, even outside the diff's hunks, so the diff alone can look the same. Nothing was written. `diff` and `writeSetDigest` are the edit as it is now.

What to do: Review `diff`, the edit as it is now; to apply it, send the request again with `expectWriteSetDigest` set to this `writeSetDigest`.

oneOf.title: Files changed while the edit was computed
oneOf.description:
A file the edit changes was changed on disk after the endpoint took its baseline, for example by another session. Nothing was written. `files` lists them.

What to do: Send the same request again: the endpoint computes the edit afresh from the files as they are now.

oneOf.title: A file of the edit couldn't be written
oneOf.description:
Writing the edit failed partway: for example, a file without write permission, or a full disk. The endpoint writes every file of an edit or none, so every file it had written was put back to its exact earlier bytes (a moved file to its old path, a created one deleted), and the worktree is as it was. `detail` has the system's error, and says if anything couldn't be put back; `files` names the file that failed.

What to do: Check the file's permissions and the disk (`detail` has the system's error), then send the same request again. Every file the edit had written was put back, unless `detail` says otherwise.

oneOf.title: Not ready
oneOf.description:
Either JDT LS is still starting (`reason: starting`), or a worktree is being imported, and imports run alone (`reason: importing`, with `worktree`). The request asked not to wait (`wait: false`), or its timeout passed while it waited. `retryAfter` is an estimate.

What to do: Wait `retryAfter` seconds and send the same request again, or send it with `wait: true`.

oneOf.title: Too many requests at once
oneOf.description:
Every one of the endpoint's 16 worker threads is taken and 64 requests already wait for one, as many as it queues; or the request was still waiting in that queue when its `timeoutMs` passed, and was answered then. Either way it wasn't run, and won't be.

What to do: Wait `retryAfter` seconds and send the same request again.

oneOf.title: The endpoint is shutting down
oneOf.description:
`POST /v1/shutdown` was called. No new work starts.

What to do: Start a new JDT LS: that's the harness's job. Don't retry against this one.

oneOf.title: The operation timed out
oneOf.description:
The operation started, but didn't finish within `timeoutMs`. The endpoint cancelled it, and wrote nothing. `phase` says where it was.

What to do: Send it again with a larger `timeoutMs`, or narrow it (a smaller `limit`, the module scope).

oneOf.title: JDT LS returned an error
oneOf.description:
The LSP passthrough's request failed in JDT LS. `lsp` has JDT LS's error code, message and data, unchanged.

What to do: Read `lsp.message`. Check the method's params against the LSP specification: positions are 0-based there.

oneOf.title: The passthrough refuses that method
oneOf.description:
The passthrough doesn't send that method or `workspace/executeCommand` command: it would break the endpoint's ownership of JDT LS (lifecycle methods, workspace folder changes, document synchronization and file events, settings, builds, notifications, and commands that change projects, the workspace, settings, the build state or files), or it's one the endpoint hasn't classified. `detail` says which, `field` points at `/method` or `/params/command`, and `hint` names what to use instead.

What to do: Use the endpoint's own operation instead: `worktrees/add` and `/remove` for folders. Files are read from disk, so there's nothing to synchronize.

oneOf.title: A URI isn't in the worktree
oneOf.description:
A `file:` URI in the passthrough's `params` is outside the worktree the request names, or a `jdt:` URI names another worktree's project. The endpoint reconciles only the named worktree with the disk, so it would answer from what may be stale. `field` points at the URI. When a registered worktree holds the file, the candidate sets `worktree` and `module` to it.

What to do: Send the request for the worktree that holds the file: apply the candidate. The endpoint reconciles only the named worktree with the disk, so a file elsewhere could be read stale.

oneOf.title: Internal error
oneOf.description:
An unexpected failure in the endpoint. Its log has the stack trace, under `instance`. The endpoint keeps serving.

What to do: Report it with `instance`. The same request may fail the same way.

element.description:
A Java name for a declaration: in the worktree's sources, or, for a read-only operation, on the requesting module's classpath.

- A type: `com.acme.Foo`. A nested type: `com.acme.Foo.Bar` (`com.acme.Foo$Bar` works too).
- A method: `com.acme.Foo#bar`, or with its parameter types, `com.acme.Foo#bar(int,java.lang.String)`.
- A constructor: the type's simple name as the member, `com.acme.Foo#Foo(int)`.
- A field or an enum constant: `com.acme.Foo#count`.
- A package: `com.acme`.

Rules:

- **Parameter types are optional.** Without them, a name that matches several overloads is `ambiguous-member`, which lists every overload: pass one back. `bar()` means no parameters.
- **Parameter types** are comma-separated, and whitespace is ignored. Each may be simple (`String`) or fully qualified (`java.lang.String`). Type arguments are ignored (`List<String>` is `List`). Arrays are `int[]`, and varargs `String...`, which is the same as `String[]`.
- **A field wins a name without parentheses:** `com.acme.Foo#size` is the field `size` if `Foo` declares one; a method that shares a field's name is written with its parentheses, `com.acme.Foo#size()`.
- **Ambiguous:** a simple parameter type that matches two types (`Date` for `java.util.Date` and `java.sql.Date`). A fully qualified parameter type matches only that type.
- **Library and JDK elements** (`java.lang.Math#max(int,int)`) can be named in the read-only operations (definition, references, implementations, type-hierarchy, call-hierarchy, describe). A name that matches nothing in the worktree's sources is looked up on the requesting module's classpath: its Maven dependencies and the JDK. Refactorings only ever address the worktree's own sources.
- **No name here:** anonymous classes, lambdas and local variables. Address them with a `TextAnchor`.
- **The fully qualified form** that results and errors use always resolves.

element.description:
A Java name for a declaration: in the worktree's sources, or, for a read-only operation, on the requesting module's classpath.

- A type: `com.acme.Foo`. A nested type: `com.acme.Foo.Bar` (`com.acme.Foo$Bar` works too).
- A method: `com.acme.Foo#bar`, or with its parameter types, `com.acme.Foo#bar(int,java.lang.String)`.
- A constructor: the type's simple name as the member, `com.acme.Foo#Foo(int)`.
- A field or an enum constant: `com.acme.Foo#count`.
- A package: `com.acme`.

Rules:

- **Parameter types are optional.** Without them, a name that matches several overloads is `ambiguous-member`, which lists every overload: pass one back. `bar()` means no parameters.
- **Parameter types** are comma-separated, and whitespace is ignored. Each may be simple (`String`) or fully qualified (`java.lang.String`). Type arguments are ignored (`List<String>` is `List`). Arrays are `int[]`, and varargs `String...`, which is the same as `String[]`.
- **A field wins a name without parentheses:** `com.acme.Foo#size` is the field `size` if `Foo` declares one; a method that shares a field's name is written with its parentheses, `com.acme.Foo#size()`.
- **Ambiguous:** a simple parameter type that matches two types (`Date` for `java.util.Date` and `java.sql.Date`). A fully qualified parameter type matches only that type.
- **Library and JDK elements** (`java.lang.Math#max(int,int)`) can be named in the read-only operations (definition, references, implementations, type-hierarchy, call-hierarchy, describe). A name that matches nothing in the worktree's sources is looked up on the requesting module's classpath: its Maven dependencies and the JDK. Refactorings only ever address the worktree's own sources.
- **No name here:** anonymous classes, lambdas and local variables. Address them with a `TextAnchor`.
- **The fully qualified form** that results and errors use always resolves.
